title: Allegory and History: How Alexandria and Antioch Read the Bible
standfirst: The Early Church and Its Readers
subtitle: Philo's Alexandrian inheritance, Origen's three senses, the Greek habit of reading Homer for hidden meaning, the Antiochene answer of historia and theoria, and the two reading cultures that still live in modern Christians.

sections.title: Two Cities, Two Habits of Reading
sections.body:
Every Christian who opens the Bible reads it through habits learned somewhere else, and almost none of us know where we learned them. We assume that our way of reading is simply reading, the obvious thing any honest person would do with an ancient book. The history of the early church makes that assumption hard to keep. Between roughly AD 200 and 450, two great cities of the eastern Mediterranean trained Christians to read the same Scriptures in recognizably different ways, and each city's habit grew out of its schools, its philosophy and its sense of what a sacred text is for.

Alexandria, on the Egyptian coast, was the intellectual capital of the Greek-speaking world, home of the great library and of a long tradition of reading old texts for hidden philosophical meaning. Antioch, in Syria, was a commercial and administrative city whose schools prized rhetoric, the disciplined study of how a speech or narrative actually works. Out of the first came a reading that searched beneath the letter for the spirit. Out of the second came a reading that insisted the spirit must be found through the history the letter records.

Readers who know the site's history of the councils will recognize these two cities as names for rival parties in the fifth-century arguments about the person of Christ. That story is real, and it is told elsewhere. This essay is about something prior and in some ways more intimate: how two Christian cultures taught believers to hear the voice of God in a text. Neither school was simply right. Each saw something the other missed, and both are still alive in the way we read on an ordinary weekday morning, usually without our noticing.

sections.title: Philo's Alexandrian Inheritance
sections.body:
The Christian school of Alexandria did not invent its method. It inherited one, and the first great practitioner was a Jew. Philo of Alexandria, who lived from roughly 20 BC to about AD 50, belonged to the city's large and learned Jewish community and spent his life reading the books of Moses in the light of Greek philosophy, especially Plato and the Stoics. He wrote long allegorical commentaries on Genesis and the rest of the Pentateuch, and he believed that Moses, rightly understood, had taught the deepest truths the philosophers later reached by other roads.

For Philo, the narratives of the patriarchs were true, but they were also more than events. Abraham's migration from Chaldea could figure the soul's departure from the life of the senses toward the knowledge of God. The garden, the rivers and the figures of the early chapters could stand for virtues, faculties of the soul and stages of moral ascent. Philo believed he was honoring Moses rather than distorting him, defending the Jewish Scriptures before educated Greeks who found parts of them crude, and showing that Israel's lawgiver deserved a place among the wise.

It is worth pausing on the irony. Philo's works survived largely because Christians copied and treasured them, while his own community's later tradition took a different path. The Christian teachers of Alexandria, Clement late in the second century and then Origen, received from this Jewish exegete a vocabulary and a set of instincts: that the text has a body and a soul, that apparent difficulties are invitations to deeper reading, and that the purpose of reading is the ascent of the mind toward God. Christian allegory began as a debt, and the church has not always remembered to whom it was owed.

sections.title: Origen and the Three Senses
sections.body:
Origen, born in Alexandria around 185 and dead around 254 after torture in the Decian persecution, was the first Christian to write a systematic account of how Scripture should be read. He was also the most prodigious biblical scholar of the early church. He compiled the Hexapla, a vast parallel edition of the Hebrew Old Testament and its Greek translations, and he preached and commented on nearly the whole Bible, first in Alexandria and then, from the early 230s, in Caesarea. Whatever else one says about his allegory, it was not the work of a man indifferent to the text.

In the fourth book of On First Principles, which survives chiefly in the Latin translation Rufinus made in 398, Origen sets out his method. Taking his cue from a reading of Proverbs 22:20 in the Greek Old Testament, which spoke of writing things down in a threefold way, and from Paul's description of the human person as spirit, soul and body in 1 Thessalonians 5:23, he argued that Scripture has three levels of meaning. The body is the plain sense, which edifies simple believers. The soul is the moral sense, which forms the one making progress. The spirit is the spiritual sense, which discloses the mysteries of Christ and the age to come to the mature.

The most daring claim in the book is that God placed stumbling blocks in the letter on purpose. Origen pointed to passages that he thought could not be true at the level of bare event, such as the first three days of creation passing with evening and morning before there was a sun, and argued that such impossibilities were meant to stop the reader and drive him toward the spiritual meaning. He did not think most of Scripture lacked a literal sense. He thought the whole of it had a spiritual one.

sections.title: Why Allegory Made Sense
sections.body:
It is easy for a modern reader to dismiss allegory as a pious evasion, a way of escaping what the text plainly says. That judgment forgets the culture in which Origen worked. For centuries before Christ, educated Greeks had been reading their own sacred text, Homer, in exactly this way. Plato had worried in the Republic that the poets told unworthy stories about the gods, and his worry set a problem for every later reader. If Homer was the schoolbook of Greece, how could a serious person honor a poem in which the gods lie, quarrel and commit adultery?

The answer the philosophical schools gave, the Stoics above all, was allegory. The quarrels of the gods could be read as the conflict of natural elements or the struggles of the soul. The wanderings of Odysseus could figure the soul's long return to its true home. In the third century, the Neoplatonist Porphyry wrote a short treatise reading a single cave in the Odyssey as an elaborate figure of the cosmos and the descent of souls. In that world, to read a revered text allegorically was the highest form of respect available, the way an educated person showed that an ancient text deserved its authority.

Christian allegory therefore did two things at once. It answered pagan critics, such as the philosopher Celsus, against whom Origen wrote a long reply, who mocked the Bible as a collection of barbarous tales. And it claimed for the church the same intellectual dignity the philosophers claimed for Homer. The Alexandrians were reading as their culture taught every serious reader to read. Their genius was to fill that borrowed form with Christ, and their danger was that the borrowed form would sometimes decide in advance what Christ could mean.

sections.title: Historia and Theoria
sections.body:
By the later fourth century a different school had taken shape in Antioch, and its teachers regarded the Alexandrian method with real alarm. Diodore of Tarsus, who taught a circle of ascetic students in Antioch before becoming bishop of Tarsus in 378, wrote a treatise, now lost, on the difference between theoria and allegory. His two most famous pupils carried the program further. Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia from 392 until his death in 428, became the most rigorous commentator of the school. John Chrysostom, a priest of Antioch who was made bishop of Constantinople in 398, became its greatest preacher.

The Antiochenes granted that Scripture speaks of Christ beyond its immediate horizon. Their complaint was that allegory dissolved the history through which God had actually acted. Theodore, commenting on Paul's use of the word allegory in Galatians 4:24, argued that Paul compared two real events and two real women and never denied that they had existed, whereas the allegorists of his day treated the Old Testament narratives as if they were dreams. The foundation of reading, for this school, was historia: the coherent sense of the text in its own setting, the author's purpose, the shape of the argument, the sequence of the story.

Upon that foundation they allowed theoria, a word meaning sight or contemplation. Theoria was the perception, within a real historical event or prophecy, of a higher reality to which it genuinely pointed, as Jonah's three days pointed to the resurrection in Matthew 12:40. The test was that the higher sense must grow out of the historical one and never cancel it. These were men trained in the rhetorical schools, Chrysostom under the pagan rhetor Libanius, and they read Scripture as a rhetorician reads a speech: as purposeful communication, addressed to real hearers, whose meaning depends on its order and its occasion.

sections.title: What Each School Saw and Missed
sections.body:
Each school deserves to be stated as its own defenders would state it. The Alexandrian would say that the Bible is one book with one divine author, that Christ is its subject from Genesis to Revelation, and that Paul himself read the rock in the wilderness as Christ in 1 Corinthians 10:4. To refuse spiritual reading, he would say, is to read the Old Testament as a Jew who has not yet met the risen Lord, and to leave whole books, Leviticus or the Song of Songs, spiritually mute for the church. That is a serious argument, and much of the church's best preaching for a thousand years depended on it.

The Antiochene would answer that God reveals himself in history, that the incarnation is an event and not an idea, and that a method which can make any text mean anything has quietly placed the reader above the Word. He would point out that allegory tends to find in Scripture what the allegorist already believes, which is exactly the danger the rule of faith was meant to restrain. That too is a serious argument. Theodore's caution about how many psalms directly prophesy Christ, and his reading of the Song of Songs as a human love poem, show the cost of his own discipline: a reading so careful about history that it could struggle to hear the New Testament's own reading of the Old.

The Alexandrians gained the unity of the canon and the hunger for God, and they paid for it with a constant temptation to arbitrariness. The Antiochenes gained the dignity of history and the voice of the human author, and they paid for it with a constant temptation to leave Christ at the edges of the Old Testament. Frances Young has argued that the difference finally lay less in theology than in the classroom, in which ancient school a man had learned to read.

sections.title: Both Cities Live in Us
sections.body:
The argument did not end in late antiquity. Theodore was condemned more than a century after his death, in the controversy over the Three Chapters, and Origen's speculative theology was condemned in the same century, yet both of their reading habits survived and are with us still. The modern historical-critical method, with its insistence on authorial intention, original setting and the integrity of each book, is a distant heir of Antioch, though it often lacks Antioch's faith. The devotional reading of many evangelical and charismatic Christians, in which a verse about Israel's wandering in the wilderness becomes a word about a personal hardship this week, is a distant and often unwitting heir of Alexandria, though it often lacks Alexandria's discipline.

I have to be careful here, because I live in both cities and so do most pastors I know. In the study I am an Antiochene, suspicious of any reading the author could not have meant. In the pulpit, on a hard Sunday, I am tempted to become an Alexandrian of the worst kind, finding in the text whatever my people need to hear, and calling it the Spirit. Neither instinct is evil. Both become dangerous when they are unexamined, when we mistake the habit of our tribe for the plain meaning of God.

What the early church finally offers is a discipline held in tension rather than a winner: the history must stand, and Christ must be heard through it. The church did not settle the question of how to read the Bible once and for all in the fifth century, and it will not settle it in ours. The question is whether we will read knowing which culture is reading through us, or whether we will keep calling our own city's habits the voice of God.

keyFigures.name: Philo of Alexandria
keyFigures.note: Jewish philosopher whose allegorical commentaries on the books of Moses gave the Alexandrian Christians their method.

keyFigures.name: Origen
keyFigures.note: Alexandrian scholar who set out the body, soul and spirit of Scripture in the fourth book of On First Principles.

keyFigures.name: Porphyry
keyFigures.note: Neoplatonist philosopher whose allegorical reading of a cave in the Odyssey shows how the Greeks read Homer.

keyFigures.name: Diodore of Tarsus
keyFigures.note: Teacher at Antioch and later bishop of Tarsus who wrote a lost treatise distinguishing theoria from allegory.

keyFigures.name: Theodore of Mopsuestia
keyFigures.note: Bishop of Mopsuestia from 392 to 428 and the most rigorous historical commentator of the Antiochene school.

keyFigures.name: John Chrysostom
keyFigures.note: Antiochene preacher, later bishop of Constantinople, who read Scripture as purposeful speech to real hearers.
